title: ACT Reading — Practice Test 6
summary: A full timed enhanced-ACT Reading test: four original passages (a city literary narrative, an economics passage on the four-day week, paired passages on subtitles and dubbing, and an astronomy passage with a data table), 36 questions in 40 minutes, with a reason for every answer choice.

blocks.text: This is a full-length practice test for the **Reading section of the enhanced ACT**: **36 questions in 40 minutes**, four passages with 9 questions each. In the real test, **27 questions are scored** and one passage is unscored, but you will not know which one, so treat every passage as if it counts. **In this practice test, all 36 questions count.** All passages and questions are original.

rows: Humanities — paired passages A and B

items: Sit in a quiet place, put your phone away and keep scrap paper and a pencil ready.
Do the whole section in one sitting. The timer starts when you press Start and the section ends automatically after 40 minutes.
Aim for about 10 minutes per passage: roughly 3–4 minutes to read and map it, then about 6 minutes for its 9 questions.
There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question. If you are stuck, eliminate what you can, guess, mark it and move on.
The score shown at the end is a **practice percentage**, not an official ACT scaled score (1–36).

questions.p:
Passage I — Literary Narrative

LITERARY NARRATIVE: This passage is from an original short story. The narrator remembers his first journey alone across Cairo by microbus.

[1] The morning my father's car finally refused to start, my sister Nour stood in the kitchen doorway eating a piece of bread and watching me panic. It was my first day at a new secondary school on the far side of the river, and until that moment I had imagined arriving in the back seat of the car, like a parcel that someone else was responsible for delivering.

[2] "Take the microbus," Nour said, as if she were suggesting that I take an umbrella.

[3] I was fifteen and had lived in Cairo my whole life, but I had lived in it the way a fish lives in a bowl: I knew every corner of our street and almost nothing beyond it. The microbuses were something I saw rather than used, white vans that swerved to the kerb, swallowed a few people and roared away with their side doors still open. I asked Nour which one to take. She was in her second year at university and crossed the city twice a day; she could have answered in one sentence.

[4] Instead she said, "Watch the people waiting. They'll tell you." Then she went to get dressed.

[5] At the corner of the main road, a dozen people stood along the pavement, and every one of them seemed to be making a strange gesture. A man in a suit held one finger pointing at the sky. A woman with a shopping bag drew a small circle in the air. Two students beside me held their hands flat and moved them gently downward, like people calming a crowd. When a van slowed, its driver glanced at the hands, nodded at some and ignored others, and the people he had nodded at climbed in. It was a language, I realised, and I was the only person on the street who could not speak it.

[6] I did what I always did when I felt foolish: I pretended. When the next van stopped, I climbed in behind the students with the flat hands, passed my coins forward along the row of shoulders the way everyone else did, and waited to see the river. Twenty minutes later I saw instead the enormous square at Ramses, with its roaring traffic and its railway station, which was nowhere near my school.

[7] I got out because everyone got out. I must have looked as lost as I felt, because an old man selling sugar-cane juice from a cart called me over and asked where I was going. When I told him, he laughed, not unkindly, and said that I had taken a good van to the wrong place. Then, between customers, he taught me. The finger pointing up meant one district and the circle another; to cross the river towards my school, I should hold out two crossed fingers and wait at a particular corner near the bridge. He made me repeat the sign until I did it properly, and he refused my money for the juice, saying that a first lesson is always free.

[8] I reached school forty minutes late and was scolded by a teacher who did not ask why. I barely heard her. All day I kept glancing down at my own hand, practising the sign under my desk.

[9] That evening I told Nour everything, expecting sympathy, or at least an apology. She listened, nodding, and then asked me which sign would take me to the Citadel. I didn't know. She asked about the university. I didn't know that either. "Then tomorrow," she said, "you'll find out."

[10] I was angry with her for a week. It seemed to me that she had let me get lost on purpose, and in a sense she had. But by the end of that month I could cross the city alone, read the hands on any corner and even, once, help a confused visitor find the van to the airport. I also noticed that the city had changed shape around me. It was no longer a bowl with our street at the bottom; it was a map, and I was somewhere on it.

[11] Years later, I asked Nour why she hadn't simply told me which van to take. She shrugged. "If I'd told you, you would have learned one route," she said. "I wanted you to learn the city."
questions.q: Which of the following best describes the passage as a whole?
c: A narrator criticises Cairo's public transport for being crowded and hard to understand.
A narrator explains why he resented his sister for many years after she refused to help him.
A narrator recalls how a confusing first journey across the city led him to greater independence and a new view of Cairo.
A narrator compares the school he used to attend with the new school across the river.
questions.e: The story follows one journey that goes wrong and what the narrator learns from it, ending with him able to "cross the city alone". The choice about resenting his sister for years fails because his anger lasted only "a week".
ce: Wrong: the hand signals are presented as a clever system to learn, not as something to criticise.
Wrong: he was angry "for a week", and in the end he understands her reason.
Right: the passage moves from his panic and wrong turn to crossing the city alone and seeing it as "a map".
Wrong: the old school is never described; the school is only the destination.

c: misread the name of the district painted on the side of the van.
was given the wrong directions by the man selling juice.
followed other passengers into a van without understanding the signals they had made.
fell asleep and missed the stop near the bridge.

suggest that he felt trapped in Cairo and wanted to leave it.
show that his parents had forbidden him to go out alone.

did not know which microbus went towards his new school.

c: believed without question.
ate hungrily.
held back a feeling.
quickly took in.

c: The narrator is scolded by a teacher for arriving late.
The narrator helps a visitor find the van to the airport.
Nour asks the narrator which sign leads to the Citadel.

Passage II — Social Science

SOCIAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about the length of the working week. The economist and the trial described are fictional.

[1] For most of the past century, the shape of the working week has seemed as fixed as the calendar itself: five days on, two days off. Yet there is nothing natural about it. In the early factories of the nineteenth century, many people worked six long days a week, and the weekend as most people know it today spread only gradually. One famous step came in 1926, when the carmaker Henry Ford adopted a five-day, forty-hour week in his factories. Four years later, the economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that, thanks to rising productivity, people a century in the future might need to work only about fifteen hours a week.

[2] That prediction has not come true. Productivity — the amount a worker produces in an hour — has risen enormously since Keynes's time, but in most countries the standard working week has barely moved in decades. Much of the gain has gone into higher incomes and more goods rather than more free time. Recently, however, a growing number of companies have begun to ask whether the old bargain could be renegotiated: the same pay for four days of work instead of five.

[3] Labour economist Rania Fouad set out to test the idea carefully. Her team recruited twenty-eight mid-sized firms — software companies, accounting offices, a furniture maker, two call centres and a chain of opticians — that agreed to try a four-day week for six months while keeping salaries unchanged. Crucially, Fouad also tracked a comparison group of similar firms that kept the five-day week, so that changes caused by the trial could be separated from changes that would have happened anyway, such as a busy season or a general rise in demand.

[4] The results were more encouraging than many managers had expected. In most of the trial firms, output per employee stayed roughly level, and in several it rose slightly. Employees reported sleeping better and feeling less exhausted, and the number of sick days fell. Perhaps most important for employers, fewer workers quit: resignations in the trial firms were noticeably lower than in the comparison group. Because finding and training a replacement is expensive, Fouad argues, keeping experienced staff can repay much of the cost of a shorter week.

[5] How could people produce as much in four days as in five? Interviews suggested that the answer lay less in working faster than in wasting less time. Teams shortened their meetings or cancelled them altogether. Managers stopped asking for reports that no one read. One accountant described the change this way: "When Friday disappeared, we finally had to decide what was actually important." In economic terms, the shorter week acted as a kind of pressure that pushed firms to remove tasks that had survived only out of habit.

[6] Fouad is quick to point out the limits of her findings. The trial firms volunteered, and companies that volunteer for such an experiment may already be well organised or unusually open to change. The gains were also far from universal. Office firms adapted most easily, while the furniture maker struggled, because its machines and workers could not simply produce a quarter more in each remaining day. One of the call centres abandoned the trial after three months: customers expected someone to answer the phone five days a week, and spreading the staff across different days off made the timetable so complicated that the savings disappeared.

[7] These differences point to a broader lesson. The four-day week is not one policy but many, and whether it succeeds depends on the kind of work involved. Where output is measured by finished tasks — a completed report, a working piece of software — reorganising time can raise efficiency. Where output depends on simply being present, such as staffing a reception desk or running a machine, fewer hours usually means less produced, unless more workers are hired.

[8] Fouad does not believe that the five-day week will disappear soon, but she thinks the question Keynes raised deserves a serious answer. "We have spent a century turning higher productivity into more things," she says. "It is at least worth asking whether some of it should be turned into more time."

Passage III — Humanities (Paired Passages)

HUMANITIES: Passage A is from an original essay by a film critic. Passage B is from an original essay by a director of film dubbing. Both writers are fictional.

PASSAGE A — "Hearing the Real Voice"

[1] The first foreign film I ever loved, I watched with subtitles, and I have distrusted dubbed versions ever since. My reason is simple: an actor's voice is not a container for the words of the script. It is part of the performance. The way a voice catches before a confession, the breath an actor takes before a lie, the rhythm of an argument that speeds up until the speakers interrupt each other — these are as carefully made as any gesture or glance.

[2] Dubbing removes all of that and replaces it with the work of someone else, recorded in a studio months later, often in a few hurried takes. Even when the new voice is skilful, it belongs to a different body. The lips on the screen move to one language while the sound arrives in another, and some part of the mind notices the mismatch, even when we try not to. A subtitled film keeps the original soundtrack whole: the voices, the silences and the background noise are exactly as the director chose. Nothing has been added that the film's makers did not intend, and nothing they intended has been taken away.

[3] People who dislike subtitles usually complain that reading distracts them from the picture. In my experience, this problem is far smaller than it sounds. Within a few minutes, most viewers stop noticing that they are reading at all; the eye learns to take in a line of text at a glance and return to the faces. Many teachers would add that children who grow up watching subtitled programmes often pick up a surprising amount of the foreign language along the way.

[4] I will not pretend that subtitles are perfect. A line of text can hold only so many words, so long speeches must be shortened, and a joke that depends on a pun may simply vanish. But a subtitle is an honest compromise. Its presence at the bottom of the screen tells you that something has been translated. A dubbed voice pretends that nothing has.

PASSAGE B — "In Defence of the Second Voice"

[1] For twenty years I have directed the dubbing of foreign films, and for twenty years critics have spoken of my work as a kind of forgery. I understand their love of the original voices. But good dubbing is not forgery; it is a craft, and like any craft it can be done well or badly.

[2] When my actors prepare a role, they watch the original performance many times. They study where the actor breathes, where the voice rises and where it breaks, and they try to rebuild that emotion in their own language. Our translators, meanwhile, have an advantage that subtitlers lack. A subtitle must be short enough to read in a few seconds, so a large part of what is said is often cut. A dubbed line can carry the whole meaning, and when a joke cannot be translated, we can write a new joke that does the same work.

[3] Subtitles also ask something of the audience that critics rarely notice, because critics are fast readers. Young children cannot follow them. Neither can many people with poor eyesight, or viewers who read slowly or not at all. For these audiences, a subtitled film is not a purer experience; it is an experience they cannot have.

[4] Even for skilled readers, subtitles have a cost. A film is first of all something to be seen. In a fast action scene, or in a shot that a director has composed with great care, every second that the eye spends at the bottom of the screen is a second it does not spend on the picture. A dubbed film leaves the eye free to follow the whole frame, from the actors' faces to the smallest detail in the background, exactly as the director arranged it.

[5] I admit that bad dubbing exists. Rushed recordings, careless translations and a single bored voice used for several characters have given my profession its poor reputation. But the answer to bad dubbing is good dubbing, not no dubbing at all.

c: dubbing should be banned from cinemas.
subtitles translate a film without losing anything.

Wrong: the author admits that speeches are shortened and puns may "vanish".
Wrong: the author defends subtitles, which are a translation.
Right: these are the author's two main reasons, in paragraphs 1–2 and paragraph 4.

public complaints.
rumours that spread quickly.
random errors or changes in the measurements.

questions.q: According to paragraph 7, the planets found by the transit method are only "a small sample" of those that exist because:
c: most planets are too far from their stars to be detected.
space telescopes have stopped watching most stars.
astronomers reject most of the candidate signals they find.
only planets whose orbits are lined up with our view pass in front of their stars as seen from Earth.
questions.e: Karimi explains that the method sees only edge-on orbits, so many planets never cross their stars from our point of view. The passage does mention false alarms, but not as the reason the sample is small.
ce: Wrong: distance from the star is not the reason given.
Wrong: the passage says nothing about telescopes stopping.
Wrong: false alarms are mentioned, but they are not the reason given for the small sample.
Right: others "pass above or below their stars" and never cast a shadow towards us.

questions.q: Karimi's statement in paragraph 7 that "we are counting the ones that happened to line up with our point of view" mainly serves to:
c: argue that transiting planets are a different kind of planet from all others.
criticise earlier astronomers for counting carelessly.
suggest that Earth has an unusual position in space.
stress that the results of the transit method depend on the observers' position.
questions.e: The quotation sums up the limit just described: what we find depends on our line of sight. Saying that transiting planets are a different kind of planet confuses a limit of the method with a property of the planets.
ce: Wrong: the point is about what we can see, not about planets being different in kind.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the explanation for EVERY question, including the ones you got right, and check the reason given for each wrong choice.
Sort your wrong answers into Key Ideas and Details, Craft and Structure, and Integration of Knowledge and Ideas. The results screen links each weak skill to a lesson.
Main idea, detail and inference mistakes: go back to "Main Idea and Summary Questions", "Detail Questions: 'According to the Passage'" and "Inference Questions: 'It Can Reasonably Be Inferred'".
Word meaning, purpose and tone mistakes: review "Words and Phrases in Context", "Purpose, Function and Text Structure" and "Point of View, Tone and Perspective".
Paired-passage, table and evidence mistakes: review "Paired Passages: Comparing Two Authors", "Passages with Charts, Tables and Graphs" and "Evaluating Arguments: Claims, Evidence and Reasoning".
If you ran out of time, re-read "ACT Reading Strategy: Read Fast, Answer Smart" and practise one passage a day with a 10-minute timer.
